stories.title: Morgan Stanley Acquires KC Ace Hardware Facility for $159M
stories.excerpt: Morgan Stanley Investment Management, through investment funds managed by Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing, acquired a newly developed 1.5 million-square-foot distribution facility in Kansas City, Missouri, for $158.5 million. The property was acquired from Hunt Midwest, which developed the logistics facility as a build-to-suit in 2025, the first phase of KCI 29 Logistics Park. The facility is subject to a long-term net lease with Ace Hardware. The property was acquired through an off-market transaction facilitated by Mark Long and John Hassler of Newmark Zimmer. “This acquisition reflects our continued conviction in high-quality net lease investments that combine strong tenant credit, mission-critical operations and institutional-quality real estate,” said David Gross, Managing Director at Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing. The Ace Hardware facility is located within KCI 29 Logistics Park, a 3,300-acre megasite, which will support up to 20 million square feet of industrial facilities. Measuring a half mile from end to end, the new facility is the largest distribution center in Kansas City by building footprint. The post Morgan Stanley Acquires KC Ace Hardware Facility for $159M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Morgan Stanley acquired 1.5M SF Ace Hardware distribution facility in Kansas City for $158.5M.
Hunt Midwest developed facility as build-to-suit; part of 3,300-acre KCI 29 Logistics Park megasite.
Largest distribution center by footprint in Kansas City; long-term net lease anchors institutional investment.
stories.summary: Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing acquired a newly built 1.5 million-square-foot logistics facility in Kansas City leased to Ace Hardware for $158.5 million. The property is the largest distribution center by building footprint in the metro and represents phase one of a 3,300-acre megasite capable of supporting 20 million square feet of industrial development. The acquisition reflects institutional appetite for high-quality net lease industrial assets with strong tenants and mission-critical operations.
stories.impact: Kansas City's logistics infrastructure expansion signals rising regional distribution demand, likely driven by Midwest supply-chain centralization and e-commerce growth. Multifamily developers should monitor job creation from the full buildout of KCI 29 (projected 20M SF) and downstream residential demand in submarkets near the Park; wage growth from logistics jobs supports rental demand and rents.

stories.title: Greenberg Traurig Hires Brian Helweil as Shareholder in Global Real Estate Practice
stories.excerpt: New York real estate attorney Brian Helweil has landed at law firm Greenberg Traurig. Helweil, an attorney with experience representing both landlords and tenants, will serve as a shareholder in the law firm’s global real estate practice in its New York office, according to a Tuesday announcement. “[Helweil] further strengthens our depth and expertise in the New York leasing market and beyond,” Richard A. Rosenbaum, executive chairman of Greenberg Traurig, said in a statement. Rosenbaum added that increasing Greenberg Traurig’s “critical mass” in New York City’s thriving office leasing market is a strategic priority for the firm. Helweil’s practice focuses on commercial office and retail leasing, as well as acquisitions, dispositions, financings and joint ventures in New York and across the U.S. He joins Greenberg Traurig from law firm Loeb & Loeb, where he spent roughly three years as a partner representing owners, developers, investors, landlords and tenants. Helweil also previously worked as an associate at Fried Frank. During his career, Halweil has represented clients in massive headquarters leases with square footages spanning six to seven figures, according to the announcement, including a 1 million-plus-square-foot headquarters lease for a multinational media and entertainment company. Helweil earned his bachelor’s degree from New York University and his juris doctor from Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law. A spokesperson for Loeb & Loeb did not respond immediately to a request for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Greenberg Traurig hired Brian Helweil as shareholder in New York real estate practice.
Helweil brings 3+ years as partner at Loeb & Loeb; practice focuses on leasing, acquisitions, financings.
Law firm prioritizing 'critical mass' in NYC office leasing market as strategic focus.
stories.summary: Law firm Greenberg Traurig hired Brian Helweil as a shareholder in its New York real estate practice. Helweil, formerly a partner at Loeb & Loeb, specializes in commercial office and retail leasing, acquisitions, and financings across the U.S. The firm explicitly stated that strengthening its NYC leasing practice is a strategic priority.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. Story reflects law firm portfolio shifts toward office leasing in a weak office market; signals no particular capital, demand, or cost signal relevant to apartment development.

stories.title: Cardone Capital Pays $89.9M for 282-Unit Naples Multifamily Community
stories.excerpt: Cardone Capital paid $89.9 million, including 282 Bitcoin, for Orchid Run, a 282-unit apartment development in Naples, Florida. The Inland Real Estate Group of Companies was the seller. Berkadia’s Matt Mitchell and Chris Burtner arranged the sale on behalf of The Inland Real Estate Group. Completed in 2015, Orchid Run is located at 10991 Lost Lake Drive in Central Naples. The garden-style community features 108 one-bedroom, 126 two-bedroom and 48 three-bedroom residences averaging approximately 1,040 square feet. Amenities include a swimming pool and spa with private cabanas, a large fitness center with a dedicated yoga studio, a sprawling clubhouse with a resident lounge and demonstration kitchen, a coffee bar, outdoor grilling and entertaining areas, a pet washing station, a car wash and gated entry. The acquisition expands Cardone Capital’s portfolio to more than 14,800 apartment units and over $5.4 billion in assets under management. bullets: Cardone Capital paid $89.9M for 282-unit Orchid Run apartment community in Naples, Florida.
Garden-style property completed in 2015; Inland Real Estate Group seller; Berkadia brokered transaction.
Acquisition grows Cardone's portfolio to 14,800+ units and $5.4B AUM; includes Bitcoin as partial consideration.
stories.summary: Cardone Capital acquired Orchid Run, a 282-unit garden-style apartment community in Central Naples, Florida, for $89.9 million (including Bitcoin as consideration). The property, completed in 2015, features one-, two-, and three-bedroom units averaging 1,040 square feet with full resort-style amenities. The acquisition expands Cardone's portfolio to over 14,800 units and $5.4 billion in assets under management.
stories.impact: Naples market continues to attract institutional capital, signaling sustained demand from wealth migration to Southwest Florida. Established communities (2015 vintage) trading at ~$319K/unit suggests pricing discipline remains despite high supply in coastal Florida; near-term development opportunity windows closing in saturated coastal submarkets as institutional buyers acquire and hold.

stories.title: Artifact Real Estate Buys Historic Odd Fellows Hall in Little Italy for $28M
stories.excerpt: An Uptown Manhattan landlord has purchased a Little Italy office building. Washington Heights-focused Artifact Real Estate Development purchased 165 Grand Street for $28 million from Bijan Nassi of Bijan Royal, according to a deed filing in property records Tuesday afternoon. Nassi, a controversial residential landlord who has fallen into poor standing with the New York City Public Advocate’s office by making the Worst Landlord Watchlist in 2025, acquired the property with an alternative address of 224 Centre Street in 1997 for an unknown amount, property records indicate. It’s unclear whether the sale is tied to a foreclosure action taken by Nassi’s lenders in June 2025 after he defaulted on an $11.4 million loan. It’s also unclear who brokered the deal. Nassi could not be reached for comment, while Artifact did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The six-story building between Centre and Baxter streets has unique Italianate style architecture, and was built around 1847. It served as the former headquarters of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows, a non-political fraternal organization, in the 1880s. It was also given protected status by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1982, which recognized the building’s history as one of the earliest extant Italianate style buildings in the city. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Artifact Real Estate purchased historic Odd Fellows Hall at 165 Grand Street in Little Italy for $28M.
Property sold from troubled landlord Bijan Nassi; sale possibly tied to June 2025 foreclosure action.
Six-story Italianate building built ~1847; unknown end use; conversion development potential unclear.
stories.summary: Washington Heights-based developer Artifact Real Estate purchased the historic Odd Fellows Hall at 165 Grand Street in Manhattan's Little Italy for $28 million. The property was acquired from landlord Bijan Nassi, who defaulted on an $11.4 million loan and faced foreclosure action in June 2025. The six-story building features unique Italianate architecture dating to approximately 1847.
stories.impact: Distressed sale signals potential for mixed-use or residential conversion in prime SoHo/Little Italy submarket, but absence of stated end-use and conversion economics unclear; minimal impact without visibility to Artifact's development plan. Watch for entitlement and conversion announcement to assess demand signal and cost structure for historic rehab multifamily in Manhattan.

stories.title: U.S. Consumer Prices Edge Up 0.1% in July; Annual Inflation Cools to 3.4%
stories.excerpt: The Consumer Price Index rose 0.1% in July, rebounding from a 0.4% decline in June, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported. Over the past 12 months, the index increased 3.4%, down slightly from 3.5% in June. Shelter costs rose 0.1% in July, accounting for roughly two-thirds of the monthly increase, while food prices also rose 0.1%, driven by a 0.3% jump in food away from home. Energy prices fell 1.5% for the month, though they remained up sharply over the trailing year. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.2% after holding flat in June, with increases in medical care, airline fares, communication, education, and recreation. Motor vehicle insurance was among the categories that declined. The core index rose 2.5% over the 12 months ending in July, down from 2.6% the prior month. The report arrives as Federal Reserve officials assess whether inflation is slowing sufficiently to keep interest rates unchanged. The Fed held its target federal funds range at 3.50% to 3.75% at its July meeting, as inflation remained above its 2% objective. The post U.S. Consumer Prices Edge Up 0.1% in July; Annual Inflation Cools to 3.4% appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: U.S. CPI rose 0.1% in July; annual inflation cooled to 3.4% YoY from 3.5% in June.
Shelter costs rose 0.1% in July, accounting for roughly two-thirds of monthly CPI increase.
Core CPI (excluding food/energy) rose 2.5% YoY; Federal Reserve holds rates at 3.50-3.75%.
stories.summary: The Consumer Price Index increased 0.1% in July, with annual inflation cooling to 3.4% from 3.5% in June. Shelter costs rose 0.1% and accounted for roughly two-thirds of the monthly increase, while core inflation (excluding food and energy) rose 2.5% year-over-year, down from 2.6%. The Federal Reserve maintained its federal funds rate target at 3.50% to 3.75% as it assesses whether inflation is slowing sufficiently.
stories.impact: Shelter inflation persistence (0.1% MoM) and core above 2% target suggest Fed rate cuts may remain delayed or measured; expect higher cap rates and borrowing costs to persist longer than hoped, compressing acquisition yields and development returns. Modestly cooling headline inflation (_3.4% vs 3.5%_) creates optionality for rate cuts by late 2025, but multifamily underwriting should assume 4.0%+ long-term cap rate environment and higher construction financing costs.

stories.title: The Plan: Extell’s 70-Unit 50 West 66th Street Leans Into Luxury Via Hospitality
stories.excerpt: Central Park views? Check. An abundance of natural light? Check. Doorman? Check. Resort-quality amenities? Check. Honestly, once you move in there’s really no reason to ever leave Extell’s 50 West 66th Street. The 70-story condominium building has two sides: the house, which has 84 units, and the tower with 37 units. Residents began moving in last year, but the building is still undergoing some finishing touches and has a few units that need to be completed. Still, Janice Chang of Douglas Elliman said most buyers purchased based solely on the renderings and floor plans, as they were so taken with the possibilities. “We’ve sold a lot of these apartments sight unseen,” Chang said. “We just started showing people the furnished models, and it’s been so well received, it’s so incredible.” The view from the tower units is nothing short of spectacular. Any of these homes — which range in size from two to six bedrooms and in price from $8 million to $85 million — would make for the perfect retreat for a snuggly day at home reading and watching the city’s activity go by. “This is the best view because it’s panoramic,” Chang said while showing Commercial Observer around a recently completed, nearly 10,000-square-foot unit. “It’s a sweep from the Hudson River all the way to Central Park South. And you’re not very high, you can see all of the trees and landmarks, and up to the George Washington Bridge.” There are touches of luxury throughout each unit, including the white marble kitchens with Miele appliances, double ovens and wine refrigerators. There’s also cabinetry by designer SmallBone, and bathrooms with heated floors, rain showers and deep-soaking tubs. (You know CO is a sucker for a good tub.) There are uniquely designed light fixtures in the units and throughout the building, almost like statement pieces in their own right, bringing more sophistication to the property. “After people move in, they tell me they love it. stories.title: Looking Past the Noise: A More Nuanced View of Multifamily
stories.excerpt: The multifamily market is entering a new phase defined less by broad national narratives and more by local realities, operational discipline, and selective opportunity. In a recent conversation on “Inside the Deal, a CRE Podcast by Berkadia®,” host Ernie Katai, executive vice president – head of production for Berkadia, sat down with rental housing economist Jay Parsons to unpack what is actually happening across multifamily today — beyond the noise of headlines and broad-brush narratives. Parsons emphasized that many common multifamily narratives are too simplistic. He noted that rental housing tends to perform best when the broader economy is strong, household formation is healthy, and consumer confidence is rising, underscoring how closely multifamily is tied to the overall state of the economy. If there is one word Parsons uses repeatedly, it is “resilient.” He described today’s apartment market as choppy and renter-favorable, but still remarkably durable. Even after the largest supply wave since the 1970s, national rent declines have remained relatively modest in aggregate, and vacancy has not deteriorated as severely as many feared. Likewise, while valuations are down from peak levels, the worst-case distress scenarios that many expected several years ago have not materialized at scale. Instead, debt availability and recapitalization have allowed many owners to hold on longer than expected, softening what could have been a far more dramatic correction. That does not mean conditions are easy. Parsons characterized the current phase as both a messy transition and a recovery — a “two steps forward, one step back” environment. Deals are getting done, but not without obstacles. bullets: Berkadia economist: multifamily market entering phase defined by local realities, not national narratives.
Rental housing described as 'choppy and renter-favorable' but 'resilient' despite largest supply wave since 1970s.
Rents declining modestly in aggregate; vacancy has not deteriorated as severely as feared.
stories.summary: In a Berkadia podcast discussion, rental housing economist Jay Parsons emphasized that multifamily narratives are overly simplistic and the market is entering a phase defined by local market conditions rather than broad national trends. Parsons described the apartment market as choppy and renter-favorable yet resilient, noting that even after the largest supply wave since the 1970s, national rent declines have remained modest and vacancy rates have not deteriorated as severely as anticipated.
stories.impact: Critical market signal: national supply saturation is real, but submarket-level dynamics differ significantly. Developers should prioritize markets with strong household formation, employer growth, and healthy consumer confidence; avoid generic supply plays in weak-demand metros. Renter favorability and modest rent declines signal consolidation phase—winners will be operators in supply-constrained, high-demand corridors; losers in saturated coastal markets.

stories.title: Law Firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee Establishes NYC Office at 7 World Trade Center

The lease establishes a New York office for the firm, an elite litigation boutique.“Dunn Isaacson Rhee represents the caliber of organization that continues to define 7 World Trade Center as one of Downtown Manhattan’s premier office destinations,” said Keith Cody, Head of Commercial Leasing at Silverstein Properties. “Today’s leading firms are seeking workplaces that reflect their brand, support their people, and provide an exceptional experience for their clients. Through thoughtful design, hospitality-driven amenities, and a commitment to excellence, 7 World Trade Center continues to deliver an environment that meets those expectations.”Tenant representation was provided by Lisa Ann Pollakowski, Cory Gahr and Richard Plehn of Lee & Associates. Silverstein positioning 7 WTC as 'premier office destination' for high-caliber professional services firms.

stories.impact: Minimal multifamily relevance. Office leasing by law firms does not inform apartment demand or supply; reflects selective strength in Downtown Manhattan office (post-WTC rebuild) but unrelated to rental housing economics or development feasibility.

stories.title: Newmark Closes Note Sale on San Pedro Adaptive Reuse
stories.excerpt: Newmark arranged the sale of a note secured by Topaz Tower, a fully entitled adaptive reuse development project located at 222 W. 6th St. in San Pedro. The 12-story, 309,732-square-foot office tower is entitled for conversion to 246 market-rate multifamily units. Executive managing director Ryan Plummer, co-head of U.S. Capital Markets Kevin Shannon, vice chairman Ken White, senior managing director Chris Benton and managing director Anthony Muhlstein represented the lender. The buyer was 222 PV Harbor View, LLC, a private Los Angeles-based residential developer. “Topaz Tower represents an exceptionally rare opportunity to acquire a fully entitled coastal high-rise multifamily conversion with scale, ocean views and an immediate execution path in a rapidly evolving submarket,” said Plummer. Topaz Tower Apartments will include a mix of studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom residences with an average unit size of 835 square feet. Planned amenities include a rooftop deck with a resort-style pool, ocean-view units, balconies and high ceilings. Stay ahead of the multifamily market at Connect Apartments. bullets: Newmark closed sale of mezzanine note on Topaz Tower in San Pedro; 246-unit entitled conversion.
12-story, 309,732 SF office tower fully entitled for adaptive reuse to market-rate apartments; 835 SF avg.

stories.summary: Newmark facilitated the sale of a note secured by Topaz Tower, a fully entitled adaptive reuse development in San Pedro, Los Angeles. The 12-story, 309,732-square-foot office building is entitled for conversion to 246 market-rate multifamily units averaging 835 square feet. The buyer, 222 PV Harbor View LLC, is a Los Angeles-based residential developer; planned amenities include rooftop pool, ocean views, and high ceilings.
stories.impact: San Pedro submarket showing traction for office-to-residential conversion with coastal positioning and scale (246 units). Entitled deals with clear execution path attracting specialized residential capital; signals conversion economics are viable in coastal LA submarkets when entitled. Developers should monitor San Pedro and similar coastal office corridors where supply is constrained, rents are rising, and entitled conversion pipelines can move quickly to capture demand.

stories.title: Venture X Coworking Location to Open in Pompano Beach
stories.excerpt: Priddy Spaces has signed a 20,000-square-foot lease for a Venture X coworking location in Pompano Beach, Fla. The coworking operator signed a 10-year lease at a 44,102-square-foot office property within Grover Corlew’s Mayla Pompano mixed-use development. Located at 2335 East Atlantic Boulevard, the four-story office building sits two blocks east of Dixie Highway and was constructed in 2020. The coworking outpost — which will span the building’s second, third and fourth floors — will feature 85 private office suites and four meeting rooms. It’s expected to open next year. “Pompano Beach is experiencing one of the most exciting transformations in South Florida,” Kevin Priddy, co-founder and CEO of Priddy Spaces, said in a statement. “The combination of new residential development, improved infrastructure, vibrant dining and retail, and its proximity to the beach has created an environment where businesses and talent want to be.” Pompano Beach, long a working-class town, is seeing a rush of luxury condo development along its coast, from the likes of Miami-based Related Group and other developers. West Palm Beach-based Priddy Spaces is a franchisee of Venture X, operating five locations in South Florida, with Vast Coworking Group serving as the franchisor. Private equity firm New State Capital Partners purchased Vast Coworking Group earlier this year for an undisclosed amount. Priddy Spaces operates a Venture X location in nearby Boca Raton at Grover Corlew’s Palmetto Central office campus. The four-acre Mayla Pompano mixed-use development includes a 355-unit apartment building and two other office properties. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Priddy Spaces signed 20K SF lease for Venture X coworking in Pompano Beach, Florida.
10-year lease; 85 private office suites + 4 meeting rooms; expected open 2026.
Coworking expansion follows Pompano Beach luxury residential boom and infrastructure improvements.
stories.summary: Priddy Spaces, a coworking operator, signed a 10-year lease for 20,000 square feet at a mixed-use property in Pompano Beach, Florida, for a Venture X location spanning three floors of a 44,102-square-foot office building. The facility will feature 85 private office suites and four meeting rooms and is expected to open in 2026. The lease reflects Pompano Beach's transformation through new residential development, infrastructure improvements, and proximity to the beach.
stories.impact: Coworking expansion in Pompano Beach signals growing white-collar workforce influx tied to residential development boom in South Florida submarket. Multifamily developers should track talent concentration—coworking facilities follow residential migration and job creation; Pompano's infrastructure and residential pipeline indicate sustained demand tailwinds for rental apartments. Proximity to luxury coastal condo development (Related Group, others) suggests mixed-income opportunity; younger workforce (coworking tenants) may anchor workforce/workforce-plus rental demand.
